## LFP vs. NMC Lithium-Ion Batteries for Electric Vehicles

### Overview and Market Trends
Lithium-ion batteries are fundamental to electric vehicles (EVs), with Nickel Manganese Cobalt (NMC) and Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP) being the two most prevalent cathode chemistries [autocarindia.com](https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-features/tech-talk-does-ev-battery-composition-matter-434419) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/). Both NMC and LFP battery demand are projected to increase [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles). The global lithium-ion battery market surpassed USD 150 billion in 2025 [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks) [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/the-rise-of-lithium-ion-batteries). EVs drive this demand, accounting for over 70% of battery deployments in 2025 [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks), and roughly 75% of global demand in 2024 [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies).

LFP batteries have been rapidly gaining market share. In 2025, LFP surpassed nickel-based chemistries to become the dominant global EV battery chemistry, with demand increasing by 48% [insideevs.com](https://insideevs.com/news/784963/lfp-overtakes-nickel-battery-chemistry/). LFP accounted for over half of global EV battery deployments in 2025 [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks) [insideevs.com](https://insideevs.com/news/784963/lfp-overtakes-nickel-battery-chemistry/) and over 50% of EV batteries in 2024 [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies). This shift is influenced by lower costs and longer cycle life [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies). China has been a leader in LFP adoption, with LFP dominating the Chinese passenger EV market by 2023 [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles). In 2024, 80% of EVs sold in China used LFP batteries [insideevs.com](https://insideevs.com/news/784963/lfp-overtakes-nickel-battery-chemistry/). While Europe and North America have historically favored NMC, LFP uptake is rising, driven by demand for lower-cost EV models [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles). Forecasts suggest LFP could capture the largest global market share before 2030 [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles).

### Performance Characteristics

**Energy Density and Range**
*   **NMC:** Generally offers higher energy density, providing longer range for EVs [autocarindia.com](https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-features/tech-talk-does-ev-battery-composition-matter-434419) [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/). Cell-level energy density for NMC can reach up to approximately 260 Wh/kg [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007), with typical ranges between 150–220 Wh/kg [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries). At the pack level, the energy density difference between NMC and LFP in real vehicles is about 5–20% [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles).
*   **LFP:** Historically has lower energy density than NMC, which translates to less range [autocarindia.com](https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-features/tech-talk-does-ev-battery-composition-matter-434419) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/). Cell-level energy density for LFP typically ranges from 90–200 Wh/kg [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries). However, advancements in LFP technology, including cell-to-pack designs, have narrowed the energy density gap [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles) [insideevs.com](https://insideevs.com/news/784963/lfp-overtakes-nickel-battery-chemistry/) [techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/24/heres-why-slate-changed-the-battery-in-its-cheap-ev-truck/). Top LFP pack energy density rose from about 80 Wh/kg in 2014 to approximately 140 Wh/kg by 2023 [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles).

**Cycle Life and Longevity**
*   **LFP:** Offers longer cycle life, often beyond 2000 cycles [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007). LFP batteries can achieve 4,000–10,000+ cycles, translating to a practical life of 15+ years [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).
*   **NMC:** Typically has a shorter cycle life, ranging from 1,500–3,000 cycles, with a typical life of 6–10 years [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).

**Thermal Stability and Safety**
*   **LFP:** Known for excellent thermal stability and enhanced safety [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007) [autocarindia.com](https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-features/tech-talk-does-ev-battery-composition-matter-434419) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/). LFP's thermal runaway onset temperature is around 270°C, and it releases significantly less energy and flammable gas during thermal events compared to NMC [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).
*   **NMC:** More prone to thermal runaway and fires when damaged, with a thermal runaway onset temperature between 150–210°C [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/).

**Charging Behavior**
*   **LFP:** Commonly supports 100% daily charging without significant impact on longevity [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/).
*   **NMC:** Often recommended to limit daily charging to around 80% to preserve battery longevity [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).

**Cold and Hot Weather Performance**
*   **NMC:** Retains 70–80% of its capacity at -20°C, generally performing better in cold weather [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).
*   **LFP:** Shows slightly weaker performance in cold temperatures but exhibits less lifespan loss in hot climates compared to NMC [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries).

### Cost and Materials
*   **LFP:** Significantly more affordable, being about 30% cheaper than comparable chemistries [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007). LFP cell production cost is approximately 20% lower than NMC under similar conditions [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles). In 2025, LFP prices fell over 15% and were more than 40% cheaper than NMC [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks) [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries). The use of LFP can cut battery costs by about 40% [techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/24/heres-why-slate-changed-the-battery-in-its-cheap-ev-truck/). LFP uses no cobalt or nickel, which are expensive and raise ethical and environmental concerns [autocarindia.com](https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-features/tech-talk-does-ev-battery-composition-matter-434419) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/).
*   **NMC:** Higher costs are associated with the use of cobalt and nickel [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007) [autocarindia.com](https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-features/tech-talk-does-ev-battery-composition-matter-434419) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/).

### Applications and Strategic Considerations
*   **LFP:** Ideal for applications prioritizing longevity, safety, and cost-efficiency [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007) [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries). It is favored for budget-friendly, standard-range EVs, city vehicles, and high-cycle use cases like fleets or taxis [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries) [autonews.com](https://www.autonews.com/ev/batteries/ane-ev-battery-chemistry-race-nickel-lithium-0407/). LFP is also dominant in Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), accounting for over 90% of the market in 2025 [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks). For heavy-duty trucks, LFP is often preferred due to durability and cost, despite lower energy density [reneweconomy.com.au](https://reneweconomy.com.au/batteries-and-cells-whether-on-wheels-or-the-grid-its-all-about-chemistry-and-cost/).
*   **NMC:** Suitable for high-power, high-energy-demand scenarios where space and weight constraints are critical, such as premium or long-range EVs [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007) [otomobilgi.com](https://otomobilgi.com/en/nmc-or-lfp-a-guide-to-electric-vehicle-battery-chemistries) [autonews.com](https://www.autonews.com/ev/batteries/ane-ev-battery-chemistry-race-nickel-lithium-0407/). It is chosen when maximizing energy density and performance at extreme temperatures is a priority [autonews.com](https://www.autonews.com/ev/batteries/ane-ev-battery-chemistry-race-nickel-lithium-0407/).

### Supply Chain and Environmental Impact
*   **Supply Chain:** The production of LFP batteries is heavily concentrated in China, which has led to concerns about supply chain resilience [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/mgi/our-research/batteries-scaling-the-engine-of-electrification) [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies). Over 70% of EVs produced outside China depend on Chinese batteries or components [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks). North America and Europe rely heavily on imports for LFP cells and midstream components [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/global-battery-markets-are-growing-strongly-and-so-are-the-supply-risks) [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/mgi/our-research/batteries-scaling-the-engine-of-electrification).
*   **Environmental Impact:** LFP batteries have a smaller carbon footprint and do not use cobalt or nickel, which have environmental and social concerns associated with their mining [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007) [autocarindia.com](https://www.autocarindia.com/auto-features/tech-talk-does-ev-battery-composition-matter-434419) [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/). NMC batteries have greater environmental concerns due to their cobalt and nickel content [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007).

### Future Outlook and Emerging Technologies
Both NMC and LFP technologies are expected to continue evolving with ongoing improvements in efficiency, safety, and cost reduction [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007) [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies). While LFP is poised to gain the largest global market share in the near future, NMC will remain essential for high-performance applications [mckinsey.com](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/automotive-and-assembly/our-insights/the-battery-chemistries-powering-the-future-of-electric-vehicles) [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fub.2024.100007).

Next-generation battery technologies are also on the horizon. Solid-state batteries, which replace liquid electrolytes with ceramic, promise reduced fire risk, lighter packs, higher energy density, faster charging, and longer life [irishtimes.com](https://www.irishtimes.com/special-reports/2026/10/23/ev-battery-jargon-buster/). However, solid-state and sodium-ion batteries currently have limited manufacturing capacity, mostly concentrated in China, and require continued research, investment, and scalable manufacturing to achieve widespread deployment [faraday.ac.uk](https://www.faraday.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/Faraday_Insights_18_FINAL.pdf) [iea.org](https://www.iea.org/commentaries/how-can-innovation-help-secure-future-battery-markets-and-mineral-supplies). These emerging chemistries are expected to grow but with varying timelines, potentially capturing a significant market share by 2040 in a scenario of rapid breakthroughs [faraday.ac.uk](https://www.faraday.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/Faraday_Insights_18_FINAL.pdf).

At the pack level, the energy density difference between NMC and LFP in real vehicles is about 5–20% [S1].
*   **LFP:** Historically has lower energy density than NMC, which translates to less range [S4][S11]. Cell-level energy density for LFP typically ranges from 90–200 Wh/kg [S9]. However, advancements in LFP technology, including cell-to-pack designs, have narrowed the energy density gap [S1][S15][S16]. Top LFP pack energy density rose from about 80 Wh/kg in 2014 to approximately 140 Wh/kg by 2023 [S1].

**Cycle Life and Longevity**
*   **LFP:** Offers longer cycle life, often beyond 2000 cycles [S3]. LFP batteries can achieve 4,000–10,000+ cycles, translating to a practical life of 15+ years [S9].
*   **NMC:** Typically has a shorter cycle life, ranging from 1,500–3,000 cycles, with a typical life of 6–10 years [S9].

**Thermal Stability and Safety**
*   **LFP:** Known for excellent thermal stability and enhanced safety [S3][S4][S11]. LFP's thermal runaway onset temperature is around 270°C, and it releases significantly less energy and flammable gas during thermal events compared to NMC [S9].
*   **NMC:** More prone to thermal runaway and fires when damaged, with a thermal runaway onset temperature between 150–210°C [S9][S11].

**Charging Behavior**
*   **LFP:** Commonly supports 100% daily charging without significant impact on longevity [S9][S11].
*   **NMC:** Often recommended to limit daily charging to around 80% to preserve battery longevity [S9].

**Cold and Hot Weather Performance**
*   **NMC:** Retains 70–80% of its capacity at -20°C, generally performing better in cold weather [S9].
*   **LFP:** Shows slightly weaker performance in cold temperatures but exhibits less lifespan loss in hot climates compared to NMC [S9].

### Cost and Materials
*   **LFP:** Significantly more affordable, being about 30% cheaper than comparable chemistries [S3]. LFP cell production cost is approximately 20% lower than NMC under similar conditions [S1]. In 2025, LFP prices fell over 15% and were more than 40% cheaper than NMC [S5][S9]. The use of LFP can cut battery costs by about 40% [S16]. LFP uses no cobalt or nickel, which are expensive and raise ethical and environmental concerns [S4][S11].
*   **NMC:** Higher costs are associated with the use of cobalt and nickel [S3][S4][S11].

### Applications and Strategic Considerations
*   **LFP:** Ideal for applications prioritizing longevity, safety, and cost-efficiency [S3][S9]. It is favored for budget-friendly, standard-range EVs, city vehicles, and high-cycle use cases like fleets or taxis [S9][S13]. LFP is also dominant in Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), accounting for over 90% of the market in 2025 [S5]. For heavy-duty trucks, LFP is often preferred due to durability and cost, despite lower energy density [S12].
*   **NMC:** Suitable for high-power, high-energy-demand scenarios where space and weight constraints are critical, such as premium or long-range EVs [S3][S9][S13]. It is chosen when maximizing energy density and performance at extreme temperatures is a priority [S13].

### Supply Chain and Environmental Impact
*   **Supply Chain:** The production of LFP batteries is heavily concentrated in China, which has led to concerns about supply chain resilience [S6][S7]. Over 70% of EVs produced outside China depend on Chinese batteries or components [S5]. North America and Europe rely heavily on imports for LFP cells and midstream components [S5][S6].
*   **Environmental Impact:** LFP batteries have a smaller carbon footprint and do not use cobalt or nickel, which have environmental and social concerns associated with their mining [S3][S4][S11]. NMC batteries have greater environmental concerns due to their cobalt and nickel content [S3].

### Future Outlook and Emerging Technologies
Both NMC and LFP technologies are expected to continue evolving with ongoing improvements in efficiency, safety, and cost reduction [S3][S7]. While LFP is poised to gain the largest global market share in the near future, NMC will remain essential for high-performance applications [S1][S3].

Next-generation battery technologies are also on the horizon. Solid-state batteries, which replace liquid electrolytes with ceramic, promise reduced fire risk, lighter packs, higher energy density, faster charging, and longer life [S11]. However, solid-state and sodium-ion batteries currently have limited manufacturing capacity, mostly concentrated in China, and require continued research, investment, and scalable manufacturing to achieve widespread deployment [S2][S7]. These emerging chemistries are expected to grow but with varying timelines, potentially capturing a significant market share by 2040 in a scenario of rapid breakthroughs [S2].

Summary:
- Raft is a consensus algorithm that yields the same results as (multi-)Paxos but is designed to be easier to understand and implement. It strengthens coherency by separating leader election, log replication, and safety, reducing state complexity.
- Key innovations:
  - Strong leader: log entries flow only from leader to followers, simplifying log management.
  - Leader election: uses randomized timers to elect leaders quickly and quietly resolve conflicts.
  - Membership changes: introduces a joint consensus mechanism where overlapping majorities across configurations maintain safety during reconfiguration.
- Usability evidence: a user study with 43 students found Raft substantially easier to understand than Paxos. On average, participants scored higher on Raft quizzes (mean Raft score ≈ 25.7 vs. Paxos ≈ 20.8 out of 60; difference ≈ 4.9 points; 95% CI indicates Raft is at least 2.5 points higher). About one-third of participants performed better on Raft; the study controlled potential biases and reported the materials for review.

Summary:
- The document outlines the core roles and operations in a Raft implementation (HashiCorp Raft).
- Key concepts:

## Raft Consensus Algorithm: Leader Election and Log Replication

The Raft consensus algorithm is designed to manage replicated logs in distributed systems, offering an understandable and implementable alternative to Paxos [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). It ensures that multiple servers agree on a sequence of commands, maintaining consistency even with server failures [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/). Raft achieves this by separating consensus into key subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/).

### Leader Election

Raft employs a strong leader model where only one leader coordinates all log replication [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

*   **Process:**
    *   Leaders are elected using randomized timers, which helps in quickly resolving conflicts and minimizing extra mechanisms [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).
    *   When a leader crashes, a new leader is elected [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
    *   During an election, a server becomes a candidate and gathers votes from peers by sending `askPeerForVote` requests [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
    *   A server votes for only one candidate per term, and this vote is persisted [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Election safety ensures that at most one candidate can win in a given term [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf)[5].
    *   Randomized election timeouts within a range (e.g., [T, 2T]) reduce the likelihood of split votes, leading to a stable leader quickly emerging [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

*   **Guarantees:**
    *   Election safety ensures that at most one candidate can win in a term [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   The system can tolerate crash failures of up to *f* replicas while still making progress, requiring a majority to be available [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

### Log Replication

Log entries in Raft flow exclusively from the leader to its followers, simplifying log management [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

*   **Process:**
    *   The leader is responsible for replicating log entries [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
    *   New entries are appended by the leader and then replicated to followers using `AppendEntries` Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   A log entry is committed when the leader that created it has successfully replicated it to a majority of its peers [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Once committed, commands are applied to the state machine, and results are returned to clients [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   The leader maintains pipelines for log replication and heartbeats [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
    *   In case of failures, the leader may send a snapshot to a follower to bring it up to date [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).

*   **Log Structure and Safety:**
    *   Each log entry consists of an index, a term, and a command [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Logs are stored durably on disk and become part of the state machine's execution [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   Raft enforces several safety guarantees for log replication:
        *   **Leader Append-Only Logs:** Leaders never overwrite existing entries in their logs [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
        *   **Log Matching:** If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, then the logs are identical in all preceding entries [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
        *   **Leader Completeness:** If a log entry has been committed in a given term, then all future leaders for that term or higher terms will have that entry in their logs [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
        *   **Commitment Consistency:** No two leaders can cause conflicting committed entries [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
        *   **State Machine Safety:** If a server has applied a log entry to its state machine, no other server will ever apply a different command for the same log index [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).

*   **Client Interaction:**
    *   Clients typically contact the leader; if the leader is unknown, requests are redirected [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   The leader responds to clients only after the command has been logged, committed, and executed by the state machine [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
    *   To achieve exact-once semantics, client requests include a unique ID to detect and safely handle duplicates [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be more understandable than Paxos while providing formal safety guarantees for non-Byzantine faults. Key points:

- Purpose: Distributes a replicated state machine across a cluster; ensures all nodes agree on the same sequence of state transitions.
- Structure: One elected leader handles log replication; followers exist to apply logs. Leaders send regular heartbeats; followers time out and trigger elections if heartbeats stop.
- Safety properties:
  - Election safety: at most one leader per term.
  - Leader append-only: leaders only add entries, never overwrite or delete.
  - Log matching: if two logs share an entry at the same index and term, their logs are identical up to that point.
  - Leader completeness: committed entries in a term are present in all leaders’ logs thereafter.
  - State machine safety: once a server applies a log entry to its state machine, others won’t apply a different command for that log.
- Fault model: Crash fault tolerance (not Byzantine) in base form; variants with cryptographic signatures can achieve Byzantine fault tolerance.
- Drawbacks:
  - Leader bottleneck: all client requests and replication pass through a single leader, creating a potential bottleneck and single point of failure in performance.
  - Reconfiguration risk: membership changes are not formally verified; past safety bugs have occurred.
- Implementations: Multiple reference implementations exist (Go, C++, Java, JavaScript, Scala).

Bottom line: Raft provides a transparent, formally proven approach to crash fault-tolerant consensus with a leader-based log replication model, but it faces bottlenecks from a single leader and lacks fully verified formal guarantees for dynamic membership changes.

## Raft Consensus Algorithm: Leader Election and Log Replication

The Raft consensus algorithm is designed to be more understandable than Paxos while achieving the same results for replicated state machines [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). It decomposes the consensus problem into distinct parts: leader election, log replication, and safety [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/).

### Leader Election

*   Raft uses randomized timers for leader election, allowing for quick and clean election of leaders [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).
*   The system ensures election safety, meaning at most one leader is elected per term [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   Leaders send regular heartbeats to followers [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). If followers do not receive heartbeats, they time out and trigger a new election [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   Raft employs a "strong leader" model, where a single leader manages log replication [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). This approach simplifies correctness and implementation [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).
*   When cluster membership changes, Raft uses a joint consensus approach, employing safe, overlapped configurations [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).

### Log Replication

*   The elected leader is responsible for handling log replication [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   The leader accepts client commands, appends them to its own log, and then replicates these entries to its followers [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf).
*   Raft ensures that leaders are append-only, meaning they cannot modify or delete their own log entries [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   The algorithm maintains log consistency through properties such as Log Matching, which states that if two logs share an entry at the same index and term, their logs are identical up to that point [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   Leader Completeness ensures that committed entries in a term are present in all subsequent leaders' logs [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   While temporary inconsistencies may occur during leader changes, logs are designed to converge to the leader's view over time [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/slides/uiuc2016.pdf).
*   A potential drawback of the single-leader model is that all client requests and replication pass through the leader, which can create a bottleneck and a single point of failure in terms of performance [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).

  - Elections: random election timeouts in [T, 2T] reduce split votes; a stable leader typically emerges quickly.

## Raft Consensus Algorithm: Leader Election and Log Replication

The Raft consensus algorithm is designed to be an understandable and implementable alternative to Paxos for managing replicated state machines [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). It aims for fault tolerance, ensuring that a cluster of servers can agree on a sequence of commands and maintain a consistent, identical log, even in the presence of failures [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/). Raft achieves this by dividing the consensus problem into three distinct subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/).

### Leader Election

Raft utilizes a strong leader model, where one leader coordinates all log entries and replicates them to followers [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). This approach simplifies log management compared to other consensus algorithms [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

*   **Randomized Timers:** Leader elections in Raft use randomized timers to quickly and quietly resolve conflicts [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf).
*   **Election Process:** When a server (follower) does not receive heartbeats from the current leader within a certain timeout, it assumes the leader has crashed and transitions to a candidate state [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). The candidate then requests votes from other servers in the cluster [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
*   **Voting:** A server votes for only one candidate per term, and this vote is persisted [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Election Safety:** Raft ensures that at most one candidate can win in a given term [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)). A stable leader typically emerges quickly due to the randomized election timeouts [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Leadership Transfer:** Raft includes mechanisms for leadership transfer and verification to maintain leadership integrity [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).

### Log Replication

In Raft, all log entries flow from the leader to its followers, simplifying the process of keeping logs consistent across the cluster [raft.github.io](https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).

*   **Log Structure:** Each log entry consists of an index, a term, and the command to be executed [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). These logs are stored durably on disk and are applied to the state machine [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Leader Append-Only:** Leaders are responsible for appending new entries to the log and replicating them to followers [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf) [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   **AppendEntries RPCs:** New log entries are appended by the leader and replicated to followers via AppendEntries Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs) [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Commitment:** A log entry is considered committed when the leader that created it has successfully replicated it to a majority of its peers [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md). Once committed, commands are applied to the state machine, and results are returned to clients [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Leader Completeness:** Committed entries in a term are guaranteed to appear in all future leaders' logs [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf)[5]. Leaders never overwrite committed entries [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf).
*   **Log Matching Property:** If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, then the logs are identical up to that point [en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raft_(algorithm)).
*   **Snapshotting and Compaction:** Raft uses snapshotting and log compaction to manage storage and performance by discarding older, committed log entries [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).
*   **Handling Failures:** If a leader crashes, a new leader is elected, and Raft's safety properties ensure consistency with previously committed entries [cs.princeton.edu](https://www.cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/spring24/cos418/docs/L13-raft.pdf). If a follower falls behind, the leader may send it the latest snapshot to help it catch up [github.com](https://github.com/hashicorp/raft/blob/main/docs/README.md).

sources.summary:
Summary:
- Raft is a consensus algorithm that yields the same results as (multi-)Paxos but is designed to be easier to understand and implement. It strengthens coherency by separating leader election, log replication, and safety, reducing state complexity.
- Key innovations:
  - Strong leader: log entries flow only from leader to followers, simplifying log management.
  - Leader election: uses randomized timers to elect leaders quickly and quietly resolve conflicts.
  - Membership changes: introduces a joint consensus mechanism where overlapping majorities across configurations maintain safety during reconfiguration.
- Usability evidence: a user study with 43 students found Raft substantially easier to understand than Paxos. On average, participants scored higher on Raft quizzes (mean Raft score ≈ 25.7 vs. Paxos ≈ 20.8 out of 60; difference ≈ 4.9 points; 95% CI indicates Raft is at least 2.5 points higher). About one-third of participants performed better on Raft; the study controlled potential biases and reported the materials for review.

Raft is a consensus algorithm designed to be easier to understand than Paxos while delivering equivalent results for replicated state machines. Key takeaways:

- Design and goals
  - Raft splits consensus into leader election, log replication, and safety to reduce complexity.
  - It aims for a stronger, more understandable structure and reduces nondeterminism compared to Paxos.

- Core innovations
  - Strong leader: a single leader controls log entries flow to followers, simplifying replication.
  - Leader election: uses randomized timers to quickly and simply elect a new leader when needed.
  - Membership changes: introduces a joint consensus approach with overlapping majorities to safely handle cluster reconfigurations.

- Usability and validation
  - User study with 43 students showed Raft is easier to understand than Paxos.
  - In the study, 33 participants outperformed on Raft quizzes compared to Paxos (Raft mean ~25.7/60 vs Paxos mean ~20.8/60).
  - The study design attempted to be fair (counterbalanced order, controls for prior experience), and results indicate a statistically supported understanding advantage for Raft.

- Practical implications
  - Raft provides an equivalent to Paxos in effect, with a clearer structure and practical mechanisms for leadership, election, and dynamic membership.
  - Its approach to log replication and safety is designed to be more approachable for building real systems.

Key takeaways: Raft provides a simple, understandable consensus protocol to replicate logs as a replicated state machine across 2f+1 servers, tolerating up to f crashes.

- Core guarantees
  - Safety: If a log entry is committed, it will be present in all future leaders’ logs; no two leaders can cause conflicting committed entries.
  - Logs: Each entry is <index, term, command>; logs are stored durably on disk and become part of the state machine execution.
  - Election safety: at most one candidate can win in a term; a server votes for one candidate per term (persisted).
  - Leader completeness: leaders never overwrite committed entries; only leader’s log can advance commitment; a leader’s log is considered canonical by followers.

- Liveness and progress
  - Elections: random election timeouts in [T, 2T] reduce split votes; a stable leader typically emerges quickly.
  - Commitment and execution: new entries are appended by the leader and replicated via AppendEntries RPCs; once committed, commands are applied to the state machine and results are returned to clients.

- Leadership and replication
  - One leader coordinates; followers replicate the leader’s log.
  - If a leader crashes, a new leader may be elected, but the safety properties ensure consistency with previously committed entries.
  - Exact-once semantics are achieved by including a unique client request ID in each command; duplicates are detected and handled safely.

- Configuration changes (joint consensus)
  - Configuration changes (e.g., adding/removing servers) are treated as log entries and require joint consensus across old and new configurations during the transition.
  - Final configuration only applies after the joint phase is committed.

- Relationship to other protocols
  - Raft “looks like a single machine” using majority (f+1 of 2f+1) progress.
  - Similar in spirit to Multi-Paxos / Viewstamped Replication, but designed for easier understanding and implementation.
  - Strong leader simplifies reasoning and recovery at the cost of requiring a leader with sufficiently up-to-date logs.

- Practical implications
  - Client interactions: clients contact the leader; if unknown, requests are redirected. The leader responds only after logging, committing, and executing the command.
  - Failure handling: the system tolerates crash failures of up to f replicas; progress relies on a majority.

In short: Raft achieves safe, replicated logging with a simple leader-based approach, handles leader changes and configuration updates via log commits, and ensures that committed state is consistently applied across all servers.

Summary:
- Prime Medicine has, for the first time, edited DNA directly inside a human body (in vivo) using prime editing.
- The target condition is Wilson disease, caused by mutations in ATP7B that impair copper elimination in the liver.
- The approach aims to rewrite the faulty gene in liver cells to remove excess copper and prevent liver/nerve damage.
- This milestone marks a significant step beyond ex vivo gene editing (editing cells outside the body and reintroducing them).
- Prime editing offers greater precision, enabling insertions, deletions, and sequence changes, which base editing cannot achieve for the common ATP7B mutations.
- The FDA has approved limited in vivo gene editing therapies (CRISPR–Cas9 and others) for other conditions; no in vivo gene-editing therapy has been approved yet. An FDA decision on an in vivo CRISPR–Cas9 therapy for hereditary angioedema is anticipated next year.

Summary: Essential results from Chapter 5 (Genome editing)

- Genome editing tools and outcomes:
  - Cre-lox: Cre recombinase rearranges DNA only at lox sites; outcomes depend on site orientation (excision, inversion, integration).
  - ZFN/TALEN: Use FokI nuclease dimerization guided by programmable DNA-binding domains; create double-strand breaks (DSBs) at target sites.
  - CRISPR-Cas9: Uses a guide RNA and PAM (NGG) to direct Cas9 to a target and create a DSB; subsequent repair via HDR (with a donor) or NHEJ (indels).
  - Base editors and prime editing: Make small, precise sequence changes without a full DSB; dead Cas proteins can modulate transcription without changing sequence.
  - Dead Cas (dCas): Represses or activates transcription without altering the DNA sequence.

- DNA repair mechanisms after editing:
  - NHEJ: Predominant repair in many cells; often yields indels (loss/gain of function depending on frame).
  - HDR: Uses a donor template to introduce precise edits; requires a donor DNA.

- Alternative editing strategies:
  - Paired nickases: Two nicks required for a DSB, reducing off-target effects.
  - GUIDE-seq, CIRCLE-seq, DISCOVER-seq: Methods to empirically identify off-target cleavage rather than rely on predictions.

- Off-target considerations:
  - Off-target cuts are a real concern; use empirical assays and careful design.
  - Mismatches near PAM-proximal seed region are less tolerated; broader chromatin context and nuclease exposure time affect specificity.

- Delivery and expression context:
  - Delivery as DNA (integrating vectors), mRNA, or ribonucleoprotein (RNP) affects duration of activity and off-target risk.
  - Somatic vs. germline edits:
    - Somatic edits affect only the treated individual (not heritable).
    - Germline edits are heritable and raise significant ethical and consent concerns; such edits in embryos or gametes are not the same as somatic edits and require careful consideration.

- Practical guidance:
  - Each editing approach has distinct repair outcomes, efficiencies, and safety considerations.
  - When planning edits, distinguish the intended allele, delivery method, and whether the edit is somatic or germline.
  - Targeted sequencing and unbiased assays are essential to verify on- and off-target effects.

## CRISPR Base Editing vs. Prime Editing

### Overview of CRISPR Editing Technologies
CRISPR-Cas9 is a foundational genome-editing tool that creates targeted double-strand breaks (DSBs) in DNA, leading to gene disruption or precise edits via DNA repair pathways [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9) [b10logy.com](https://b10logy.com/biotechnology/5-genome-editing/). Base editing (BE) and prime editing (PE) are advanced CRISPR-derived methods that expand the scope of genome editing by enabling precise DNA modifications without creating DSBs [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9). This reduces the incidence of indel mutations and off-target effects often associated with DSB-based methods [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

### Base Editing (BE)
Base editing facilitates precise single-base transitions, such as converting C to T or A to G [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).

**Mechanism and Capabilities:**
*   BE uses a catalytically impaired Cas protein (e.g., Cas9 nickase) fused to a deaminase enzyme [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   It directly alters a single DNA base without cutting both strands of the DNA helix or requiring a donor DNA template [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   Cytosine base editors (CBEs) convert C•G base pairs to T•A, while adenine base editors (ABEs) convert A•T base pairs to G•C [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

**Advantages:**
*   High precision for point mutations [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   Reduced generation of undesirable insertions or deletions (indels) compared to traditional CRISPR-Cas9, as it avoids DSBs [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   Has shown progress in therapeutic applications, with base editors being explored in human trials for conditions like sickle cell disease and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-026-01548-7).

**Limitations and Challenges:**
*   Limited to specific base-to-base conversions (C-to-T or A-to-G) [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   Efficiency can be variable and often lower than classic CRISPR-Cas9 [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   PAM (Protospacer Adjacent Motif) and target-site limitations restrict where edits can be made [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   Potential for "bystander" edits where unintended bases within the editing window are also modified [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   CBEs tend to have higher off-target effects than ABEs [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

### Prime Editing (PE)
Prime editing offers a broader range of edits, including all 12 possible base-to-base conversions, as well as targeted insertions and deletions [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).

**Mechanism and Capabilities:**
*   PE combines a Cas nickase (which cuts only one DNA strand) with a reverse transcriptase enzyme [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   It uses a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) that not only guides the Cas nickase to the target site but also carries the desired edited sequence as a template for the reverse transcriptase [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   This allows for the direct "writing" of new genetic information into the target DNA strand [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   PE can create targeted insertions, deletions, and all types of point mutations without relying on DSBs or separate donor DNA templates [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   New PE variants, such as TwinPE, GRAND, and PRIME-Del, can achieve large insertions and deletions, with deletions up to approximately 1 kilobase demonstrated with efficiencies up to 28% and low indel rates [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   Even larger deletions (e.g., 16.8 Mb regions) have been achieved with methods like PEDAR/bi-WT-PE, showing therapeutic potential in vivo [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).

**Advantages:**
*   Versatile editing capabilities, including all 12 base-to-base conversions, small insertions, and small deletions [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   Does not require DSBs or external donor DNA templates, reducing the risk of random integration and off-target effects [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   Generally shows lower off-target editing than Cas9 at known sites in early methods [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   Has achieved in vivo DNA editing in humans for conditions like Wilson disease, targeting mutations that base editing cannot address [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03371-x).

**Limitations and Challenges:**
*   PAM and target-site limitations can still constrain editing locations [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   Editing efficiency can vary by locus and cell type [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   Newer, more efficient PE variants (PEn, uPEn) can sometimes have off-target levels similar to Cas9 alone, necessitating careful pegRNA design and high-fidelity systems [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).
*   Requires optimization for in vivo delivery and safety [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/).

### Comparative Summary
| Feature                  | Base Editing (BE)                               | Prime Editing (PE)                                                               |
| :----------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Edit Type**            | Precise single-base substitutions (C to T, A to G) [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9) | All 12 base-to-base conversions, targeted insertions, and deletions [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9)    |
| **DSB Required**         | No [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9)                                     | No [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9)                                                                      |
| **Template Required**    | No external donor template [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624)                 | pegRNA serves as template [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9)                                               |
| **Mechanism**            | Cas protein + deaminase [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624)                    | Cas nickase + reverse transcriptase [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624)                                         |
| **Range of Edits**       | Limited to transitions [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624)                     | Broad, including transversions, indels, and larger deletions/insertions [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9) |
| **Off-target Effects**   | Can occur; CBEs potentially higher than ABEs [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) | Generally lower than Cas9 in early methods; some newer variants comparable to Cas9 [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11853414/) |
| **Efficiency**           | Variable, often lower than classic CRISPR [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624)  | Varies by locus and cell type [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9)                                               |
| **Clinical Status**      | In human clinical trials [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41573-026-01548-7)                   | First in vivo human trial initiated [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03371-x)                                         |

*   New PE variants, such as TwinPE, GRAND, and PRIME-Del, can achieve large insertions and deletions, with deletions up to approximately 1 kilobase demonstrated with efficiencies up to 28% and low indel rates [S2].
*   Even larger deletions (e.g., 16.8 Mb regions) have been achieved with methods like PEDAR/bi-WT-PE, showing therapeutic potential in vivo [S2].

**Advantages:**
*   Versatile editing capabilities, including all 12 base-to-base conversions, small insertions, and small deletions [S3].
*   Does not require DSBs or external donor DNA templates, reducing the risk of random integration and off-target effects [S1][S3].
*   Generally shows lower off-target editing than Cas9 at known sites in early methods [S2].
*   Has achieved in vivo DNA editing in humans for conditions like Wilson disease, targeting mutations that base editing cannot address [S5].

**Limitations and Challenges:**
*   PAM and target-site limitations can still constrain editing locations [S1].
*   Editing efficiency can vary by locus and cell type [S3].
*   Newer, more efficient PE variants (PEn, uPEn) can sometimes have off-target levels similar to Cas9 alone, necessitating careful pegRNA design and high-fidelity systems [S2].
*   Requires optimization for in vivo delivery and safety [S2].

| Feature                  | Base Editing (BE)                               | Prime Editing (PE)                                                               |
| :----------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Edit Type**            | Precise single-base substitutions (C to T, A to G) [S1][S3] | All 12 base-to-base conversions, targeted insertions, and deletions [S1][S3]    |
| **DSB Required**         | No [S1][S3]                                     | No [S1][S3]                                                                      |
| **Template Required**    | No external donor template [S1]                 | pegRNA serves as template [S2][S3]                                               |
| **Mechanism**            | Cas protein + deaminase [S1]                    | Cas nickase + reverse transcriptase [S1]                                         |
| **Range of Edits**       | Limited to transitions [S1]                     | Broad, including transversions, indels, and larger deletions/insertions [S2][S3] |
| **Off-target Effects**   | Can occur; CBEs potentially higher than ABEs [S1] | Generally lower than Cas9 in early methods; some newer variants comparable to Cas9 [S2] |
| **Efficiency**           | Variable, often lower than classic CRISPR [S1]  | Varies by locus and cell type [S3]                                               |
| **Clinical Status**      | In human clinical trials [S4]                   | First in vivo human trial initiated [S5]                                         |

Summary: Essential results from Chapter 5 (Genome editing)

- Genome editing tools and outcomes:
  - Cre-lox: Cre recombinase rearranges DNA only at lox sites; outcomes depend on site orientation (excision, inversion, integration).
  - ZFN/TALEN: Use FokI nuclease dimerization guided by programmable DNA-binding domains; create double-strand breaks (DSBs) at target sites.
  - CRISPR-Cas9: Uses a guide RNA and PAM (NGG) to direct Cas9 to a target and create a DSB; subsequent repair via HDR (with a donor) or NHEJ (indels).
  - Base editors and prime editing: Make small, precise sequence changes without a full DSB; dead Cas proteins can modulate transcription without changing sequence.
  - Dead Cas (dCas): Represses or activates transcription without altering the DNA sequence.

- DNA repair mechanisms after editing:
  - NHEJ: Predominant repair in many cells; often yields indels (loss/gain of function depending on frame).
  - HDR: Uses a donor template to introduce precise edits; requires a donor DNA.

- Alternative editing strategies:
  - Paired nickases: Two nicks required for a DSB, reducing off-target effects.
  - GUIDE-seq, CIRCLE-seq, DISCOVER-seq: Methods to empirically identify off-target cleavage rather than rely on predictions.

- Off-target considerations:
  - Off-target cuts are a real concern; use empirical assays and careful design.
  - Mismatches near PAM-proximal seed region are less tolerated; broader chromatin context and nuclease exposure time affect specificity.

- Delivery and expression context:
  - Delivery as DNA (integrating vectors), mRNA, or ribonucleoprotein (RNP) affects duration of activity and off-target risk.
  - Somatic vs. germline edits:
    - Somatic edits affect only the treated individual (not heritable).
    - Germline edits are heritable and raise significant ethical and consent concerns; such edits in embryos or gametes are not the same as somatic edits and require careful consideration.

- Practical guidance:
  - Each editing approach has distinct repair outcomes, efficiencies, and safety considerations.
  - When planning edits, distinguish the intended allele, delivery method, and whether the edit is somatic or germline.
  - Targeted sequencing and unbiased assays are essential to verify on- and off-target effects.

Summary:
- Base editing (BE) and prime editing (PE) are DSB-free CRISPR approaches that use catalytically impaired Cas proteins (e.g., dCas9 or nCas9 variants) to achieve precise genetic changes without double-strand breaks.
- BE enables single-base substitutions, while PE (nCas9-H840A fused to reverse transcriptase) enables targeted insertions, deletions, and point mutations at specific loci.
- BE/PE offer improvements over traditional DSB-dependent CRISPR by reducing indels and off-target effects, with reported indel rates for cytosine base editors (CBE) at ~1.1% and adenine base editors (ABE) ≤0.1%, compared with higher rates in DSB methods.
- Off-target editing exists for BE/PE, with CBE generally showing more off-target mutations than ABE; high-fidelity Cas9 variants and additional UgI strategies have been used to mitigate this.
- HF-BE variants (e.g., HF-BE2, HF-BE3) demonstrate substantially reduced off-target editing. Multiplex UgI strategies and other modifications further lower unintended edits.
- PE, in early reports, shows low off-target effects at major loci (≤0.6% in four major sites) but requires broader genome-wide assessment to fully characterize off-target risk.
- BE and PE have rapidly advanced, with broad adoption across animal, plant, and bacterial systems, driving potential in synthetic biology, agriculture, and bio-production. However, challenges remain in target-site constraints, editing efficiency, and comprehensive off-target profiling, especially for PE in bacteria/plants. The review emphasizes ongoing need for deeper mechanistic understanding and broader optimization to maximize BE/PE utility in diverse organisms.

Summary:
- The article reviews how CRISPR/Cas systems separate target binding (locator) from genetic editing (effector) modules, enabling diverse and precise genome editing technologies.
- Two main advancements are highlighted:
  - Base editors (BEs): fuse CRISPR/Cas with nucleobase deaminases to achieve single-base changes, with potential for correcting disease mutations; however, they can cause genome-wide/off-target edits via the deaminase component, independent of gRNA/Cas targeting.
  - Prime editors (PEs): fuse CRISPR/Cas with reverse transcriptases to enable a wide range of edits, including all base substitutions and small insertions/deletions, though PE design is complex (requires careful tuning of PBS length, RT template, edit position) and genome-wide off-target effects have not been fully characterized.
- The review emphasizes off-target concerns unique to BEs and discusses strategies to reduce these effects, while acknowledging ongoing challenges for in vivo use and clinical translation.
- Overall, CRISPR-conjugated base editing and prime editing represent rapid, versatile advances in genome engineering with broad therapeutic potential but require careful design and further safety evaluation.

Summary:
- Base editors (BEs) and prime editors (PEs) based on CRISPR/Cas enable efficient, double-strand-break–free genome editing.
- BEs: 
  - Cytosine base editors (CBEs) convert C to T.
  - Adenine base editors (ABEs) convert A to G.
  - Glycosylase base editors (GBEs) convert C to G.
  - Dual-base editors (DBEs) achieve simultaneous C→T and A→G edits.
  - Advanced systems like GBE2.0 achieve up to ~31% C→G efficiency; indirect deamination cannot achieve certain A-base transversions needed for ~25% of human pathogenic SNVs.
  - SWISS system enables C→T, A→G, and indels with notable efficiencies; triple-edit combination ≈7.3% co-occurrence.
- PEs (pegRNA-guided prime editing):
  - Use nCas9 fused to reverse transcriptase with pegRNA to write new sequence without DSBs.
  - First-gen PE1 showed modest efficiency (0.7%–5.5% for point mutations; 4%–17% for indels); room for improvement.
  - PE3 improves efficiency (up to ~78% in some cells like human 293T) but increases risk of indels due to two sgRNAs.
- Enhancements:
  - Mismatch repair (MMR) inhibition (e.g., MLH1dn) can boost editing efficiency in several cell types.
- Delivery:
  - Adeno-associated virus (AAV) delivery is common but limited by ~4.7 kb cargo; many BEs exceed this size.
  - Strategies to overcome size limits include splitting BEs into two AAVs and co-delivery.
- Applications and outlook:
  - BEs and PEs enable efficient genome editing across animals, plants, and microorganisms with high precision and without DSBs.
  - Ongoing work focuses on expanding base editing scopes, improving mutation efficiencies, reducing off-target effects, and advancing delivery methods for broader therapeutic use.

- Core message: Base and prime editing enable double-strand–break–free introduction of point mutations and small indels, enabling large-scale, in situ functional annotation of genetic variants (including variants of uncertain significance) and mapping of mutational landscapes.
- Key applications:
  - Systematic genotype-to-phenotype mapping to characterize disease-relevant variants.
  - High-throughput functional genomics screens that reveal mechanisms of drug resistance, immune evasion, and fundamental biology.
  - Functional annotation of noncoding elements (e.g., cis-regulatory elements) and synonymous/nondisruptive mutations.
- Methods and technology:
  - Massively parallel, densely tiled editing strategies in native genomic contexts.
  - Use of base editors (C→T, A→G conversions) and prime editors for precise sequence changes without double-strand breaks.
  - High-resolution mapping at single-nucleotide resolution to identify critical residues and regulatory sites.
- Challenges and outlook:
  - Bystander edits and unintended modifications within editing windows.
  - Efficiency limitations of HDR-based approaches in traditional CRISPR edits; reliance on DSB-free editing to avoid DNA damage responses.
  - Need for next-generation editors and integration with advanced technologies to interpret complex physiological contexts.
- Impact: Precision editing screens are redefining interpretation of genetic variation, accelerating translation to precision diagnostics and therapeutics.

Here's a one-page report on how CRISPR base editing differs from prime editing:

## CRISPR Base Editing vs. Prime Editing

### Overview and Mechanism

Base editing (BE) and prime editing (PE) are advanced CRISPR-Cas-based genome editing techniques that enable precise genetic modifications without introducing double-strand breaks (DSBs) in the DNA [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7). Both methods utilize catalytically impaired Cas proteins, such as dCas9 or nCas9 variants, to minimize unwanted DNA damage [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).

**Base Editing (BE)**
*   **Mechanism:** BE systems fuse a CRISPR/Cas protein (e.g., dCas9 or nCas9) with a nucleobase deaminase [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes). The deaminase directly converts one base to another without breaking both DNA strands [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes).
*   **Edit Types:** BE primarily introduces single-base substitutions [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
    *   Cytosine base editors (CBEs) convert C to T [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   Adenine base editors (ABEs) convert A to G [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   Glycosylase base editors (GBEs) convert C to G [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
    *   Dual-base editors (DBEs) can achieve simultaneous C→T and A→G edits [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
*   **Components:** Fuses a CRISPR/Cas protein with a deaminase [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes).

**Prime Editing (PE)**
*   **Mechanism:** PE uses an nCas9 variant fused to a reverse transcriptase (nCas9-H840A) [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624). It employs a prime editing guide RNA (pegRNA) that both guides the Cas protein to the target site and provides a template for the new DNA sequence through reverse transcription [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7). This "search-and-replace" mechanism rewrites genomic DNA without DSBs or donor DNA [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).
*   **Edit Types:** PE is more versatile, enabling a broader range of precise edits, including all 12 types of base-to-base substitutions, small insertions, and small deletions [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).
*   **Components:** Fuses nCas9-H840A with a reverse transcriptase and uses a pegRNA [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).

### Precision, Off-Target Effects, and Efficiency

Both BE and PE aim to improve precision and reduce off-target effects compared to traditional DSB-dependent CRISPR methods [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).

**Base Editing (BE)**
*   **Indel Rates:** Cytosine base editors (CBE) have reported indel rates around 1.1%, while adenine base editors (ABE) have rates of ≤0.1% [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624). These are generally lower than DSB methods [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Off-Target Effects:** Off-target editing exists for BE, with CBEs generally showing more off-target mutations than ABEs [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes). This can occur via the deaminase component independently of gRNA/Cas targeting [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes). Strategies like high-fidelity Cas9 variants (e.g., HF-BE2, HF-BE3) and multiplex UgI strategies have been developed to reduce these unintended edits [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624).
*   **Efficiency:** Advanced systems like GBE2.0 have achieved up to ~31% C→G efficiency [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).

**Prime Editing (PE)**
*   **Indel Rates:** PE is designed to have a reduced risk of indels [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z).
*   **Off-Target Effects:** Early reports suggest low off-target effects for PE at major loci (≤0.6% in four major sites), but broader genome-wide assessment is still needed [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes).
*   **Efficiency:** First-generation PE1 showed modest efficiency (0.7%–5.5% for point mutations; 4%–17% for indels) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7). PE3 has improved efficiency (up to ~78% in human 293T cells) but may increase the risk of indels due to the use of two sgRNAs [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7). Mismatch repair (MMR) inhibition can boost PE efficiency [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).

### Applications and Challenges

Both technologies have broad applications in synthetic biology, agriculture, and bio-production, and are being explored for therapeutic use [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes).

**Base Editing (BE)**
*   **Applications:** Primarily used for correcting disease-causing point mutations that require single-base substitutions (e.g., C→T, A→G) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/abstract/S0968-0004(26)00029-0).
*   **Limitations/Challenges:** Target-site constraints, editing efficiency, and comprehensive off-target profiling remain challenges [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624). Some A-base transversions needed for about 25% of human pathogenic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) cannot be achieved by indirect deamination [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7). Delivery of some BEs can be limited by the ~4.7 kb cargo capacity of AAV vectors, requiring strategies like splitting the editor into two AAVs [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).

**Prime Editing (PE)**
*   **Applications:** Enables versatile, precise edits including substitutions, insertions, and deletions, making it suitable for a wider range of genetic modifications [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9) [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41576-026-00965-z) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/abstract/S0968-0004(26)00029-0). It is particularly useful when precise insertions or deletions are needed [nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0561-9).
*   **Limitations/Challenges:** PE design is more complex, requiring careful tuning of the primer binding site (PBS) length, reverse transcriptase (RT) template, and edit position [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes). Comprehensive genome-wide off-target effects have not been fully characterized [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624) [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/trends/biochemical-sciences/fulltext/S0968-0004(20)30150-X?rss=yes). Efficiency and target-site constraints remain areas for optimization, especially in bacteria and plants [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2405805X20300624). Delivery challenges, similar to BE, also exist due to size constraints [cell.com](https://www.cell.com/molecular-therapy-family/nucleic-acids/fulltext/S2162-2531(25)00325-7).
